title: People turn again
hookLine: human life shrinks, then people turn back to goodness; Metteyya will come
carry: glad to see each other alive

cards: The Cakkavatti Sihanada keeps going down. With every new kind of wrongdoing, the story says, human lifespans shrink, from tens of thousands of years down to just ten. Fine foods disappear.
Even the idea of a good deed disappears; there's not even a word for good. People treat each other like animals.
Then comes what the text calls a sword-interval: seven days in which people see each other as prey, and kill. It's a dark page. It isn't the end.

teach.b: During those seven days, some people slip away. They hide in long grass, in thickets, in forests, among rocks and rivers, living on roots and fruit.
When the seven days are over, they come out, see each other, and embrace.

teach.h: HOW GOOD TO SEE YOU ALIVE.
teach.b: The story gives their words simply: how good to see living beings still alive! Then they talk. We lost so much because we took up wrong ways.
What if we gave up just one thing? What if we stopped killing? And they do.
Just that one. Their children live longer than they did. Seeing this, they give up something else: taking what isn't given.
Then sexual misconduct. Then lying, slander, harsh speech, and on down the list.

teach.h: ONE GOOD THING AT A TIME.
teach.b: Each generation adds one good thing, and human life lengthens again, all the way back to eighty thousand years.
Then, the Buddha says, a Buddha named Metteyya will arise in the world, as I have arisen now.
He will teach the same Dhamma, good in the beginning, the middle and the end, and lead a community of many thousands, as I lead hundreds. Two things stand out.
The turn starts with one small change, made by frightened people who are simply glad to see each other alive. Not a hero, not a king. And the hope is long.
Under his Sanskrit name, Maitreya, the Buddha to come is honored in lands far from where this was first told. Some readers hear in the name Metteyya the word metta, loving-kindness.
After all that darkness, the future has a kind name.

how: Buddhist traditions across Asia honor Metteyya, or Maitreya, as the coming Buddha, sometimes shown seated with feet on the ground, ready to rise, and some Buddhists make merit in the hope of meeting his teaching.

o: the name of the Buddha who is to come
the Buddha's own family name at birth
a title for any senior monk

games.q: people turn again: tap the pairs.
p: hid in forests and came out

s: the turn back to goodness starts with a great king
it starts with frightened survivors who agree to stop killing.
in DN 26, Metteyya will lead a community of thousands
the Buddha says, as I now lead hundreds.
human life lengthens all at once
each generation adds one good thing, and life lengthens step by step.

games.q: you've survived seven days of violence by hiding in the forest. you come out and meet other survivors. what happens?
o: you embrace, glad they're alive, and agree to stop killing.
you go back into hiding for good.
games.why: they embrace, say how good it is to see living beings, and give up killing. one good change starts the turn.

practice: Let the picture of the survivors come: people stepping out of the forest, seeing each other, glad, and breathe with that gladness.
Then look forward with hope rather than worry, and picture one good change that could spread, one generation adding one thing, maybe one you could start. Rest with that future for a while.

wordCard.voice: Metteyya, the Buddha to come: after the worst, survivors give up killing, then one wrong after another, and life grows long until he arrives. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Metteyya (Sanskrit Maitreya): the Buddha to come, named in DN 26. some readers link the name with metta, loving-kindness.

carryVoice: Your line: glad to see each other alive. Even the darkest page in the story turns on one small change. I'm glad you came.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 26 (Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta), the sword-interval, the return to goodness and Metteyya
